chapter_title: Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today
learning_objective: The learner will differentiate twelve predictions by how each answer is produced, as an oracle's answer, a cycle model, or a learned model, sorting at least 10 of the 12 correctly on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** oracle-gears-or-data-sorter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** differentiate
**Learning Objective:** The learner will differentiate twelve predictions by how each answer is produced, as an oracle's answer, a cycle model, or a learned model, sorting at least 10 of the 12 correctly on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** the oracle consultation and the Pythia (Chapters 17 and 18); the Antikythera mechanism, the Saros cycle, the four-year games cycle, Babylonian eclipse records, the parapegma, and ancient prediction machines (Part One above); machine learning and the predictive model (Chapter 19). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of the 12 statement cards in one of three bins and presses Check. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct bin" column in Content. Mastery is at least 10 of 12 correct on the first Check. Reading the bin definitions and re-sorting after the first Check are practice, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Anything ancient is guesswork or religion, so the mechanism and the Babylonian tables belong with the oracle. (2) Any machine that predicts must have learned from data, so the mechanism belongs with the learned models. (3) The bin depends on the material, clay, stone, bronze or software, rather than on the method that produced the answer. **Instructional Rationale:** Differentiating is an Analyze task: the learner must look past the surface of each source (its age, its material, its prestige) to the process behind the answer. Sorting a mixed set, with the reason shown for each card, makes that process the deciding feature. **Content:** The three bins, each shown with its one-line definition: - **Oracle:** a person gives an answer that the people asking must interpret. - **Cycle model:** a rule built from regular cycles counted in past records, fixed in advance and the same for everyone. - **Learned model:** a rule that a computer adjusted for itself from a very large number of past examples. | # | Statement shown to the learner | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Athens's envoys are told to trust the "wooden wall" (480 BCE). | Oracle | The Pythia's words came through a person, and the Assembly had to argue over what they meant. | | 2 | The mechanism's lower back dial marks a possible eclipse in a month 18 years from now. | Cycle model | The 223-month Saros cycle is cut into the gears, so the dial gives the same answer every time the crank is turned. | | 3 | A phone keyboard suggests the next word of a message home. | Learned model | The keyboard learned which words usually follow which from an enormous amount of text. | | 4 | Croesus is told that if he attacks Persia, he will destroy a great empire. | Oracle | The answer came from the Pythia, and Croesus heard the reading he wanted. | | 5 | A Babylonian scribe's clay tablet lists the months, years ahead, when an eclipse may occur. | Cycle model | It counts the same repeating cycles as the gears; the method, not the material, decides the bin. | | 6 | A bank's fraud system flags a card payment in Arachova as possibly not ours. | Learned model | The fraud check learned from millions of past genuine and fraudulent payments. | | 7 | King Laius is told that his son will kill him. | Oracle | A personal answer from Delphi, given by a person and fulfilled in the story of Oedipus. | | 8 | The mechanism's games dial shows that the Olympic Games fall in this year. | Cycle model | The four-year cycle of the games is fixed in the gearing. | | 9 | A chatbot answers the question "Will the museum be open on Monday?" | Learned model | It predicts a likely answer from its training text; it cannot know this Monday's hours. | | 10 | A stone peg calendar says that a certain star rises today and that a west wind will blow. | Cycle model | The parapegma counts the yearly cycle of star risings; its weather forecast was tied to that cycle. | | 11 | Chaerephon is told that no one is wiser than Socrates. | Oracle | An answer from the Pythia that Socrates spent his life interpreting and testing. | | 12 | A map app predicts how long the drive back from Delphi will take. | Learned model | It learned travel times from the movements of many other phones. | Bin counts: Oracle 4 (cards 1, 4, 7, 11); Cycle model 4 (cards 2, 5, 8, 10); Learned model 4 (cards 3, 6, 9, 12). **Provenance:** Cards 1, 4, 7 and 11 are the oracle stories told in Chapter 17. Cards 2, 5, 8 and 10 come from this chapter's sections "The Antikythera Mechanism" and "Ancient Prediction Machines" and from the appendix "Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism". Cards 3, 6, 9 and 12 are the everyday predictions described in Chapter 19 (Parts Two and Eight) and Chapter 2. **Rules:** Each card belongs to exactly one bin. The 12 cards are presented in a shuffled order that is fixed for each session. Check is available only when all 12 cards are placed. Only the first Check is scored. After the first Check, wrongly placed cards are marked and may be moved again for practice; a later Check reports the practice result but does not change the first-attempt score. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the three bin definitions and the question "How was each answer produced?" 2. The learner places each card in a bin. A placed card can be moved freely before Check. 3. The learner presses Check. Each card is marked correct or not yet correct, and its "Why" text appears. 4. The learner moves any wrongly placed cards and presses Check again for practice. 5. The learner should notice that cards 2, 5, 8 and 10 share a bin although they are made of bronze, clay and stone. **Feedback:** One scored attempt for all 12 cards, then unlimited practice. For each correct card: "Correct: " followed by the card's Why text. For each wrong card: "Not quite: " followed by the card's Why text; if a cycle-model card was put with the oracle, add "Ancient does not mean guesswork: this answer was counted, not revealed."; if a cycle-model card was put with the learned models, add "This rule was set once by its maker and never adjusted itself." After the first Check the score "First attempt: n of 12" is shown, and at 10 or more the message "You can tell an oracle, a cycle model, and a learned model apart by how they work." **Starting State:** The 12 cards are in a stack, the three bins are empty with their definitions visible, and the question "How was each answer produced?" is shown. **Chapter Anchors:** Three ways of predicting. Twelve statements, four per bin. The Saros is 223 lunar months, about 18 years. The games dial follows a four-year cycle. Mastery is 10 of 12.
